audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-dominant, initial: root-initial stress with proclitics outside the domain, non-strict) rests on the fieldworker's full reference grammar, and the deciding quotation is verbatim at the cited section (locator should be tightened to p. 82, pdf p. 118). The source PDF was not held before this audit; it is now on file together with the 2007 revised draft, which repeats the section unchanged, so the blank evidence grade can be raised to primary-grammar/quote-verified. No better or competing description of Skou stress exists (the tone paper and acoustic appendix are silent on stress; no instrumental stress study found). One caution worth carrying in the record: Donohue states stress is phonetically weak (slight vowel lengthening) and easily masked by lexical tone in this tone language, so 'initial stress' is a low-salience property, not a robust accentual system. sources.citation: Donohue, Mark. 2004. A grammar of the Skou language of New Guinea. Ms. dated 3 October 2004, National University of Singapore. MPG PuRe item_402710 (823 pp PDF).
sources.quote: 'In a monomorphemic word stress is on the initial syllable ... On these words stress is realised as a slight lengthening of the vowel in the stressed syllable. Stress is thus completely predictable, and is assigned to the first syllable in a simple word. In a word with proclitics, we find that stress remains on the first syllable of the root ... sources.quote: Identical wording to the 2004 version: initial stress in simple words, root-initial with proclitics outside the stress domain, no shift under reduplication or suffixation; stress weak relative to tone.
